etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin sēnsibilis (“perceptible by the senses, having feeling, sensible”), from sentiō (“to feel, perceive”).

definitions.definition: Acting with or showing good sense; able to make good judgements based on reason or wisdom, or reflecting such ability.

quote.citation: 2005, Plato, translated by Lesley Brown, Sophist, page 230b:
quote.text: They ask questions of someone who thinks he's got something sensible to say on some matter when actually he hasn't.

definitions.definition: Characterized more by usefulness, practicality, or comfort than by attractiveness, formality, or fashionableness, especially of clothing.

quote.citation: 1985, "Weird Al" Yankovic (lyrics and music), “Dare to Be Stupid”, in Dare to Be Stupid, performed by "Weird Al" Yankovic:
quote.text: Settle down, raise a family, join the PTABuy some sensible shoes and a Chevrolet

quote.citation: 1999, Neil Gaiman, Stardust (2001 Perennial Edition), page 8,
quote.text: They would walk, on fair evenings, around the village, and discuss the theory of crop rotation, and the weather, and other such sensible matters.

definitions.definition: (especially formally) Able to be sensed by the senses or the psyche; able to be perceived.

quote.citation: 1751, John Arbuthnot, An Essay Concerning the Effects of Air on Human Bodies, page 1:
quote.text: Air is sensible to the Touch by its Motion, and by its Resistance to Bodies moved in it.

quote.citation: 1778, William Lewis, The New Dispensatory, page 91:
quote.text: The sensible qualities of argentina promise no great virtue of this kind; for to the taste it discovers only a slight roughishness, from whence it may be presumed to be entitled to a place only among the milder corroborants.

quote.citation: 1902, William James, “Lecture III: The Reality of the Unseen”, in The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature […] , New York, N.Y.; London: Longmans, Green, and Co. […], →OCLC, page 54:
quote.text: It has been vouchsafed, for example, to very few Christian believers to have had a sensible vision of their Saviour.

quote.citation: 1690, William Temple, Miscellanea. The Second Part. […], London:  […]  T. M. for Ri[chard] and Ra[lph] Simpson, […], →OCLC, section III, page 207:
quote.text: [T]he diſgrace was more ſensible than the pain.

quote.citation: 1776 March 9, Adam Smith, chapter 11, in An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations. […], volume I, London:  […]  W[illiam] Strahan; and T[homas] Cadell, […], →OCLC, book I (Of the Causes of Improvement in the Productive Powers of Labour, […]), page 241:
quote.text: The discovery of the mines of America  […]  does not seem to have had any very sensible effect upon the prices of things in England.

quote.citation: c. 1608–1609 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Coriolanus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:
quote.text: Would your cambric were sensible as your finger.

definitions.definition: (archaic) Liable to external impression; easily affected; sensitive.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene viii]:

definitions.definition: (archaic) Of or pertaining to the senses; sensory.
(archaic) Cognizant; having the perception of something; aware of something.

quote.citation: 1689 (indicated as 1690), [John Locke], chapter I, in An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding. […], London:  […]  Eliz[abeth] Holt, for Thomas Basset, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: He cannot think at any time, waking or sleeping, without being sensible of it.

quote.citation: 1723, Cotton Mather, “Agathangelus; or, The Servant of God with His Guardian”, in Cœlestinus. A Conversation in Heaven, Quickened and Assisted, with Discoveries of Things in the Heavenly World. […], Boston, Mass.:  […]  S[amuel] Kneeland, for Nath[aniel] Belknap, […], →OCLC, page 2:
quote.text: A bright Meſſenger from Heaven, made the Man of GOD ſenſible, That a Remarkable Safety ſhould be granted unto him, and therefore unto all the Company vvith Him.

quote.citation: 1749, [John Cleland], “[Letter the First]”, in Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure [Fanny Hill], volume I, London:  […]  [Thomas Parker] for G. Fenton [i.e., Fenton and Ralph Griffiths] […], →OCLC, pages 213–214:
quote.text: Diſingaging myſelf then from his embrace, I made him ſenſible of the reaſons there vvere for his preſent leaving me; on vvhich, tho' reluctantly, he put on his cloaths vvith as little expedition, hovvever, as he could help, vvantonly interrupting himſelf betvveen vvhiles, vvith kiſſes, touches, and embraces, I could not refuſe myſelf to;  […]

quote.citation: 1810, Thomas Green, Extracts from the diary of a lover of literature:
quote.text: we are now sensible that it would have been absurd

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book II”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Our temper changed  […]  which must needs remove the sensible of pain.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) That which impresses itself on the senses; anything perceptible.

quote.text: Aristotle distinguished sensibles into common and proper.

quote.citation: 2018, Richard F. Hassing, Final Causality in Nature and Human Affairs (page 4)
quote.text: Accordingly, with respect to their knowability or opinability, Socrates makes no distinction among the sensibles between natural things and artifacts (510a5–6); both are relegated to the realm of opinion. Hence, there is no Socratic-Platonic biology.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) That which has sensibility; a sensitive being.

quote.citation: 1624, Democritus Junior [pseudonym; Robert Burton], The Anatomy of Melancholy: […], 2nd edition, Oxford, Oxfordshire:  […]  John Lichfield and James Short, for Henry Cripps, →OCLC:
quote.text: This melancholy extends itself not to men only, but even to vegetals and sensibles.
